{{Short description|Mathematical method}}
In [[functional analysis]], a branch of mathematics, a '''selection theorem''' is a theorem that guarantees the existence of a single-valued [[selection function]] from a given [[Set-valued function|set-valued map]]. There are various selection theorems, and they are important in the theories of [[differential inclusion]]s, [[optimal control]], and [[mathematical economics]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Fixed Point Theorems with Applications to Economics and Game Theory|last=Border|first=Kim C.|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1989|isbn=0-521-26564-9}}</ref>

== Preliminaries ==
Given two sets ''X'' and ''Y'', let ''F'' be a [[set-valued function]] from ''X'' and ''Y''. Equivalently, <math>F:X\rightarrow\mathcal{P}(Y)</math> is a function from ''X'' to the [[power set]] of ''Y''.

A function <math>f: X \rightarrow Y</math> is said to be a '''selection''' of ''F'' if

: <math>\forall x \in X: \,\,\,  f(x) \in F(x) \,.</math>

In other words, given an input ''x'' for which the original function ''F'' returns multiple values, the new function ''f'' returns a single value. This is a special case of a [[choice function]].

The [[axiom of choice]] implies that a selection function always exists; however, it is often important that the selection have some "nice" properties, such as [[continuous function|continuity]] or [[measurable function|measurability]]. This is where the selection theorems come into action: they guarantee that, if ''F'' satisfies certain properties, then it has a selection ''f'' that is continuous or has other desirable properties.

== Selection theorems for set-valued functions ==

The [[Michael selection theorem]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Michael|first1=Ernest|year=1956|title=Continuous selections. I|journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]|series=Second Series|volume=63|issue=2|pages=361–382|doi=10.2307/1969615|jstor=1969615|mr=0077107|author1-link=Ernest Michael|hdl=10338.dmlcz/119700|hdl-access=free}}</ref> says that the following conditions are sufficient for the existence of a [[Continuous function|continuous]] selection:

* ''X'' is a [[paracompact]] space;
* ''Y'' is a [[Banach space]];
* ''F'' is [[Hemicontinuity|lower hemicontinuous]];
* for all ''x'' in ''X'', the set ''F''(''x'') is nonempty, [[Convex set|convex]] and [[Closed set|closed]].

The '''approximate selection theorem'''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shapiro |first=Joel H. |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/984777840 |title=A Fixed-Point Farrago |date=2016 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-319-27978-7 |pages=68–70  |oclc=984777840}}</ref> states the following:<blockquote>Suppose ''X'' is a compact metric space, ''Y'' a non-empty [[Compact space|compact]], [[Convex set|convex]] subset of a [[normed vector space]], and Φ: ''X →'' <math>\mathcal P(Y)</math> a multifunction all of whose values are compact and convex. If graph(Φ) is closed, then for every ε > 0 there exists a continuous function ''f'' : ''X'' → ''Y'' with graph(''f'') ⊂ [graph(Φ)]<sub>ε</sub>.</blockquote>Here, <math>[S]_\varepsilon</math> denotes the <math>\varepsilon</math>-dilation of <math>S</math>, that is, the union of radius-<math>\varepsilon</math> open balls centered on points in <math>S</math>. The theorem implies the existence of a continuous ''approximate'' selection.

Another set of sufficient conditions for the existence of a continuous approximate selection is given by the '''Deutsch–Kenderov theorem''',<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|last1=Deutsch|first1=Frank|last2=Kenderov|first2=Petar|date=January 1983|title=Continuous Selections and Approximate Selection for Set-Valued Mappings and Applications to Metric Projections|journal=SIAM Journal on Mathematical Analysis|volume=14|issue=1|pages=185–194|doi=10.1137/0514015}}</ref> whose conditions are more general than those of Michael's theorem (and thus the selection is only approximate):

* ''X'' is a [[paracompact]] space;
* ''Y'' is a [[normed vector space]];
* ''F'' is ''almost lower hemicontinuous'', that is, at each {{nowrap|<math>x \in X</math>,}} for each neighborhood <math>V</math> of <math>0</math> there exists a neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>x</math> such that {{nowrap|<math display="inline">\bigcap_{u \in U} \{F(u)+V\} \ne \emptyset</math>;}}
* for all ''x'' in ''X'', the set ''F''(''x'') is nonempty and [[Convex set|convex]].

In a later note, Xu proved that the Deutsch–Kenderov theorem is also valid if <math>Y</math> is a locally convex [[topological vector space]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Xu|first1=Yuguang|date=December 2001|title=A Note on a Continuous Approximate Selection Theorem|journal=Journal of Approximation Theory|volume=113|issue=2|pages=324–325|doi=10.1006/jath.2001.3622|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The '''Yannelis-Prabhakar selection theorem'''<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Yannelis|first=Nicholas C.|last2=Prabhakar|first2=N. D.|date=1983-12-01|title=Existence of maximal elements and equilibria in linear topological spaces|journal=[[Journal of Mathematical Economics]]|volume=12|issue=3|pages=233–245|doi=10.1016/0304-4068(83)90041-1|issn=0304-4068}}</ref> says that the following conditions are sufficient for the existence of a [[Continuous function|continuous]] selection:

* ''X'' is a [[paracompact]] [[Hausdorff space]];
* ''Y'' is a [[linear topological space]];
* for all ''x'' in ''X'', the set ''F''(''x'') is nonempty and [[Convex set|convex]];
* for all ''y'' in ''Y'', the inverse set ''F''<sup>−1</sup>(''y'') is an [[open set]] in ''X''.

The [[Kuratowski and Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem]] says that if ''X'' is a [[Polish space]] and <math>\mathcal B</math> its [[Borel set|Borel]] [[Sigma-algebra|σ-algebra]], <math>\mathrm{Cl}(X)</math> is the set of nonempty closed subsets of ''X'', <math>(\Omega, \mathcal F)</math> is a [[measurable space]], and <math>F : \Omega \to \mathrm{Cl}(X)</math> is an {{nowrap|<math>\mathcal F</math>-weakly}} measurable map (that is, for every open subset <math>U \subseteq X</math> we have {{nowrap|<math>\{\omega \in \Omega : F(\omega) \cap U \neq \empty \} \in \mathcal F</math>),}} then <math>F</math> has a [[Choice function|selection]] that is {{nowrap|<math>(\mathcal F, \mathcal B)</math>-[[measurable function|measurable]].}}<ref>V. I. Bogachev, [https://www.springer.com/math/analysis/book/978-3-540-34513-8 "Measure Theory"] Volume II, page 36.</ref>

Other selection theorems for set-valued functions include:
* [[Bressan–Colombo directionally continuous selection theorem]]
* [[Castaing representation theorem]]
* [[Fryszkowski decomposable map selection]]
* [[Helly's selection theorem]]
* [[Zero-dimensional Michael selection theorem]]
* [[Robert Aumann measurable selection theorem]]

== Selection theorems for set-valued sequences ==
* [[Blaschke selection theorem]]
* [[Maximum theorem]]
